Covariance choices¶

Back to Quantile Regression

The sampling variability of a quantile-regression coefficient depends on how densely the observations lie around the fitted quantile line: where the data are sparse the line is poorly determined. The standard errors therefore rest on an estimate f₀ of the density of the residuals at zero, reported as residual_density0. It is computed by an Epanechnikov kernel with the Hall–Sheather bandwidth scaled by the smaller of the standard deviation of y and the interquartile range of the residuals divided by 1.34, so a few outliers do not inflate it.

enum class reg::QuantileCovariance { Robust, Iid };

Choice

Covariance of the coefficients

Iid

τ(1 − τ) (X′X)⁻¹ / f₀², which assumes the density of the errors near the line is the same at every x

Robust (default)

(X′X)⁻¹ X′DX (X′X)⁻¹ / f₀², a sandwich in which D has the diagonal entry τ² for an observation above the line and (1 − τ)² for one below it

The p-values and intervals use Student’s t distribution on df_resid degrees of freedom, as in least squares.

The two estimators differ except at the median¶

At τ = 0.5 the two weights τ² and (1 − τ)² are both 0.25, the sandwich collapses and the two estimators coincide exactly. For any other τ they differ, by an amount that depends on how the signs of the residuals are spread across the predictors. The program prints both standard errors at three quantiles.

#include <pluss/ma.h>
#include <pluss/tils/aux/output.h>

namespace reg = pluss::subsp::stats::regression;
using namespace pluss::tils;

int main() {
  OutputEngine out;
  out.print_defaults(PrintOptions{}.fixed(5));
  std::vector<double> xs, ys;
  for (int i = 0; i < 60; ++i) {
    const double x = 1.0 + i * 0.25;
    xs.push_back(x);
    const double noise = 2.0 * std::fmod(i * 0.6180339887498949, 1.0) - 1.0;  // a fixed low-discrepancy sequence in [-1, 1)
    ys.push_back(1.0 + 2.0 * x + x * noise);
  }
  const auto x = pluss::make_series(xs, {60, 1}, as_f64());
  const auto y = pluss::make_series(ys, {60}, as_f64());

  out.writeln("  tau   f0      Robust std errors          Iid std errors");
  for (double tau : {0.1, 0.5, 0.9}) {
    reg::QuantileOptions robust;
    robust.tau = tau;
    reg::QuantileOptions iid = robust;
    iid.covariance = reg::QuantileCovariance::Iid;
    const auto a = reg::quantile_fit(y, x, robust);
    const auto b = reg::quantile_fit(y, x, iid);
    out.writeln(tau, a.residual_density0, a.std_errors.pull<double>(), b.std_errors.pull<double>(), " same coefficients:", a.coefficients.sub(b.coefficients).abs().max().item<double>());
  }
}

Output

  tau   f0      Robust std errors          Iid std errors
0.10000 0.04626 [1.91930, 0.20624] [1.82312, 0.19337]  same coefficients: 0.00000
0.50000 0.06945 [2.02398, 0.21468] [2.02398, 0.21468]  same coefficients: 0.00000
0.90000 0.04759 [2.00456, 0.21660] [1.77201, 0.18795]  same coefficients: 0.00000

The coefficients are identical for both choices, since only the precision depends on covariance. At τ = 0.5 the two estimators agree exactly (2.02398 and 0.21468). At τ = 0.1 and 0.9 the robust standard errors are larger than the iid ones (1.919 against 1.823, and 2.005 against 1.772): the iid formula assumes the same density of errors near the line at every x, which these data, with noise that grows with x, do not satisfy. The density at zero, f₀, is largest at the median (0.069) and smaller in the tails.

Recomputing both estimators¶

Given the reported f₀ and the residuals, both formulas are a few lines of matrix algebra. The program rebuilds the two covariance matrices at τ = 0.75 and compares them with covariance and std_errors, then rebuilds the p-values from the t distribution.

#include <pluss/ma.h>
#include <pluss/tils/aux/output.h>

namespace reg = pluss::subsp::stats::regression;
namespace linalg = pluss::subsp::math::linalg;
namespace distr = pluss::subsp::stats::distr;
using namespace pluss::tils;

int main() {
  OutputEngine out;
  out.print_defaults(PrintOptions{}.fixed(6));
  std::vector<double> xs, ys;
  for (int i = 0; i < 60; ++i) {
    const double x = 1.0 + i * 0.25;
    xs.push_back(x);
    const double noise = 2.0 * std::fmod(i * 0.6180339887498949, 1.0) - 1.0;  // a fixed low-discrepancy sequence in [-1, 1)
    ys.push_back(1.0 + 2.0 * x + x * noise);
  }
  const auto x = pluss::make_series(xs, {60, 1}, as_f64());
  const auto y = pluss::make_series(ys, {60}, as_f64());
  const double tau = 0.75;

  reg::QuantileOptions robust;
  robust.tau = tau;
  reg::QuantileOptions iid = robust;
  iid.covariance = reg::QuantileCovariance::Iid;
  const auto a = reg::quantile_fit(y, x, robust);
  const auto b = reg::quantile_fit(y, x, iid);

  const auto design = pluss::series::ones({60, 1}, as_f64()).unite({x}, 1);
  const auto bread = linalg::inverse(design.transpose(0, 1).matmul(design));
  const double f0 = a.residual_density0;

  const auto iid_cov = bread.mul(tau * (1.0 - tau) / (f0 * f0));
  const auto weight = a.residuals.gt(0.0).where(pluss::series::full({60}, tau * tau / (f0 * f0), as_f64()), pluss::series::full({60}, (1.0 - tau) * (1.0 - tau) / (f0 * f0), as_f64()));
  const auto robust_cov = bread.matmul(design.transpose(0, 1).matmul(design.mul(weight.reshape({60, 1})))).matmul(bread);
  out.writeln("Iid:    largest |covariance - tau(1-tau)(X'X)^-1/f0^2|", b.covariance.sub(iid_cov).abs().max().item<double>());
  out.writeln("Robust: largest |covariance - sandwich|              ", a.covariance.sub(robust_cov).abs().max().item<double>());
  out.writeln("std errors are the square roots of the diagonals:     ", a.std_errors.sub(a.covariance.diagonal().sqrt()).abs().max().item<double>());

  const distr::StudentT t(static_cast<double>(a.df_resid), 0.0, 1.0);
  out.writeln("df_resid", a.df_resid, " p values", a.p_values.pull<double>(), " by hand", t.cdf(a.t_values.abs()).neg().add(1.0).mul(2.0).pull<double>());
  out.writeln("t values are coefficients over standard errors:", a.t_values.sub(a.coefficients.div(a.std_errors)).abs().max().item<double>());
}

Output

Iid:    largest |covariance - tau(1-tau)(X'X)^-1/f0^2| 0.000000
Robust: largest |covariance - sandwich|               0.000000
std errors are the square roots of the diagonals:      0.000000
df_resid 58  p values [0.731409, 0.000000]  by hand [0.731409, 0.000000]
t values are coefficients over standard errors: 0.000000

Both covariance matrices are rebuilt from the reported f₀ and the residuals and agree with the library’s to six decimals. The standard errors are the square roots of the diagonals, the t values are the coefficients over the standard errors, and the p-values are the two-sided tails of Student’s t on 58 degrees of freedom (60 observations less 2 parameters).

Scale¶

A quantile fit is equivariant to the scale of the response: multiplying y by 2 doubles the coefficients and halves the density of the residuals at zero, which also shows what f₀ measures: the larger the spread of the data about the line, the smaller the density at the line, and the larger the standard errors. The standard errors double with them, so the t statistics do not change. The program checks both estimators.

#include <pluss/ma.h>
#include <pluss/tils/aux/output.h>

namespace reg = pluss::subsp::stats::regression;
using namespace pluss::tils;

int main() {
  OutputEngine out;
  out.print_defaults(PrintOptions{}.fixed(6));
  std::vector<double> xs, ys;
  for (int i = 0; i < 60; ++i) {
    const double x = 1.0 + i * 0.25;
    xs.push_back(x);
    const double noise = 2.0 * std::fmod(i * 0.6180339887498949, 1.0) - 1.0;  // a fixed low-discrepancy sequence in [-1, 1)
    ys.push_back(1.0 + 2.0 * x + x * noise);
  }
  const auto x = pluss::make_series(xs, {60, 1}, as_f64());
  const auto y = pluss::make_series(ys, {60}, as_f64());
  for (auto covariance : {reg::QuantileCovariance::Iid, reg::QuantileCovariance::Robust}) {
    reg::QuantileOptions options;
    options.tau = 0.25;
    options.covariance = covariance;
    const auto base = reg::quantile_fit(y, x, options);
    const auto doubled = reg::quantile_fit(y.mul(2.0), x, options);
    out.writeln(covariance == reg::QuantileCovariance::Iid ? "Iid:   " : "Robust:");
    out.writeln("  coefficients ratio ", doubled.coefficients.div(base.coefficients).pull<double>());
    out.writeln("  f0 ratio           ", doubled.residual_density0 / base.residual_density0);
    out.writeln("  std errors ratio   ", doubled.std_errors.div(base.std_errors).pull<double>());
    out.writeln("  largest change in a t value", doubled.t_values.sub(base.t_values).abs().max().item<double>());
  }
}

Output

Iid:   
  coefficients ratio  [1.999999, 2.000000]
  f0 ratio            0.500000
  std errors ratio    [2.000000, 2.000000]
  largest change in a t value 0.000000
Robust:
  coefficients ratio  [1.999999, 2.000000]
  f0 ratio            0.500000
  std errors ratio    [2.000000, 2.000000]
  largest change in a t value 0.000000

Doubling the response doubles the coefficients (to the tolerance of the iteration), halves f₀ exactly, and doubles the standard errors, so every t statistic is unchanged. This holds for both estimators.
